Load mahou:basics first. Then read `.mahou/canvas.md` if present.

# Canvas

## Documents

A canvas is one document, `<name>.tldr.json`, in a folder a loading skill names along with the name. When the user types the skill, the folder is `canvas/` in the change's scratch folder and the document is named after what it draws. A folder can hold several documents.

- `<name>.tldr.json` is the document. The server holds it while the canvas runs and saves every edit to it, from any tab. Its `canvasVersion` names its format.
- `<name>.svg` is its export, next to it.
- `mockups/` holds the mockups every document in the folder can draw, one `<kind>.tsx` file each. A mockup is the content of the canvas's custom `mock` shape, for anything the stock tldraw shapes do not draw, such as a screen. Its file exports `mockup`, a `MockDefinition<Props>` from `@canvas/MockShape`: its natural width, its default props and a function that renders them. The natural width can also be a function of the props, for a mockup whose views have different widths. A click that changes the natural width resizes the shape by the same ratio, so the drawing keeps its scale. The canvas draws a mockup with no natural width, such as the built-in `area`, at the shape's own size instead of scaling it, so its border and label keep their size however large the shape is. A `mock` shape's `data` is merged over the defaults, so a shape passes only what differs, such as `{ kind: 'login', data: { state: 'error' } }`. A `mock` shape draws its kind at the natural width and scales the drawing to the shape's size, so one mockup renders at any shape size. Adding, changing or removing a file in `mockups/` redraws the shapes in every open tab without reloading the page.

## Running it

`scripts/canvas.sh` runs the app over one document. Pass it the document's path:

- `start` installs the app on first run, starts a detached server for the document on the first free port from 5190 and prints the URL to give the user. A document that already has a server gets its URL back. Each document has its own server, so several canvases run at once, in one project or in several; `CANVAS_PORT` picks the port instead. It refuses a document saved in an older format and names the `migrate` command.
- `watch` prints one line per event: `click` for each "Send to Agent" click, and `voice: <message>` for each voice message, with the shapes selected when it was sent.
- `export` writes `<name>.svg`.
- `texts` prints every canvas text and arrow label, one per line.
- `migrate` brings an older document to the current format, keeping the original as `<name>.tldr.json.bak`. Run it with the server stopped. When it warns that a mockup received a variant string, rewrite that mockup to read its props from `data`.
- `stop` stops the document's own server and leaves every other canvas running.

Edits to the app under `scripts/app/` reach the running canvas only after a restart, because `start` copies the app into the cache. Run `stop` and then `start`, and reload the open tabs.

Build and edit the canvas from scripts run with `agent-browser` in your own tab, opened once on `<URL>?user=Agent` and kept open, so the user sees your cursor under that name. Every tab edits the same document live: your changes appear in the user's tab as you make them, and theirs in yours. The page exposes `window.editor`, `window.tldraw` with `createShapeId` and `toRichText`, and `window.canvas` with `notes()`, `step(at, change, pause?)` and the drawing helpers below.

Draw in steps the user can follow. A script's changes reach the other tabs together, so a script that draws everything at once shows the user only the finished result. Run each element as an awaited `canvas.step`: it moves your cursor to `at` (a shape id or a page point, or `null` to stay), applies `change`, and waits `pause` milliseconds, 500 by default. One step per shape, arrow or move, in the order a person would draw them: follow the flow the drawing explains, and join each element to what it connects to as soon as both are on the canvas, so the drawing grows as one connected piece and never as all the boxes first and all the arrows last.

- An area goes first, before what it holds.
- After the first element, each new element is followed right away by the arrow that joins it to what is already drawn, then by that arrow's label if it has one.
- A note goes right after the element it describes, and its arrow right after the note.

Draw a large batch in one script instead, without `canvas.step`, when a change creates or redraws many shapes at once, such as every tree rebuilt from a revised record. Stepping through hundreds of shapes makes the user wait for a drawing they will read only once it is finished.

Check every change with a screenshot, saved under a new file name each time, since reading a path you read before can show the earlier image.

## Helpers

The helpers load with the page, so they are back after agent-browser relaunches its browser and you reopen the tab. Each helper takes a shape name and builds the shape id from it with `id(name)`, so one name reaches the same shape through every helper. Each helper that creates a shape runs as one `step`, so the user sees it arrive, and takes an optional `pause`.

The helpers keep the layout with one rule. A shape belongs to the innermost area that holds its top edge. When no area holds it, it belongs to the lowest area of its column whose top edge is above the shape's top edge. An area nested inside another area does not count in that case, so a shape placed under a nested area belongs to the area around it. To place a new shape inside a nested area, pass `into: '<area>'` to the helper that creates the shape. The area grows to hold the shape's top edge before the helper creates the shape. `flow` does the same for a column of shapes. When a shape's height changes, the shapes under it in the same area move by the same amount. The shape's area grows or shrinks to keep a 40-unit margin under the area's lowest shape. An area that sits strictly between another area's left and right edges belongs to that area, even when the inner area starts below the outer area's bottom edge. Growing the outer area does not move the nested area, and the outer area grows to hold the nested area. When an area's height changes, the areas under it in the column move, each with its shapes and the areas nested in it. A nested area that grows moves only the areas under it inside the same outer area; the outer area then grows and moves the areas under it. Place a new shape under the last one in its area, and the helpers grow the area and move the areas under it.

| Helper | What it does |
|---|---|
| `id(name)` | The shape id for a name. |
| `bounds(name)` | The shape's page bounds. |
| `plain(name)` | Reads the shape's text back as plain text, with its line breaks. Use it to edit a text in place instead of keeping a copy of the text in a script. |
| `area(name, { x, y, w, h, label, focus? }, pause?)` | Creates an `area` with its label and sends it to the back. With a name that exists, replaces the label, such as a branch's status, keeping the focus it had. `focus: true` focuses the area, as `focus` does, on creation or along with the label change. |
| `focus(name, pause?)` | Focuses the named `area`: its border turns solid red while every other area's stays grey and dashed. Only one area is focused at a time, so every other area loses the focus. With `null`, clears the focus from every area. |
| `text(name, { x, y, w, text, mono?, size?, into? }, pause?)` | Creates a text of a fixed width, in the hand font or in monospace with `mono: true`. With a name that exists, replaces the text, and moves or widens it when `x`, `y` or `w` are given. With `into`, the named area grows to hold the new shape before the helper creates the shape, so the shape belongs to that area. |
| `card(name, { x, y, w, text, color?, dash?, fill?, mono?, into? }, pause?)` | Creates a rectangle holding a text and fits its height to the text. The rectangle is violet with a semi fill by default. Use it for a question card, a summary box (`color: 'grey', fill: 'solid'`) or a monospace table (`mono: true`). With a name that exists, replaces the text and fits the height to it again. With `into`, the named area grows to hold the new shape before the helper creates the shape, so the shape belongs to that area. |
| `box(name, { x, y, w, h, text, geo?, color?, fill?, dash?, into? }, pause?)` | Creates a diagram node of a fixed size with its text centred. `geo` is `rectangle` (the default), `ellipse` or `cloud`. Use it for the parts of a diagram, coloured by the deployable they belong to. Use `card` for text that sets its own height. With a name that exists, replaces the text. With `into`, the named area grows to hold the new shape before the helper creates the shape, so the shape belongs to that area. |
| `arrow(name, from, to, { text?, bend?, labelPosition?, color?, dash? }, pause?)` | Creates an arrow bound to the centres of the shapes `from` and `to`, so the arrow follows either shape when that shape moves. With a name that exists, changes only the options given. |
| `mermaid(name, { x, y, source }, pause?)` | Creates a `mermaid` shape and sizes it to the diagram's `viewBox`, one canvas unit per diagram unit, once the diagram has rendered. With a name that exists, replaces the source and sizes the shape again. |
| `mock(name, { x, y, w?, kind, data, into? }, pause?)` | Creates a `mock` shape of the given kind with its `data`, 520 units wide unless `w` sets another width, and fits its height to the content. With a name that exists, replaces the `data` and fits the height again. With `into`, the named area grows to hold the new shape first. |
| `note(name, { x, y, w, text }, pause?)` | Creates or updates an Agent note, a grey dashed `card` labelled "Agent". The helper adds the label, so `text` holds only the message. |
| `followUp(name, { summary, note, question? })` | Fills a card with its follow-up under the card's own text: a summary box, an Agent note and, when given, the next question as a card. Replaces the parts of an earlier follow-up. The parts move with the card. |
| `fit(name)` | Zooms to the shape and sets its height from what it holds: a card or a note from its text and its follow-up, a `mermaid` shape from its diagram's `viewBox`, any other `mock` from its `data-root` element scaled from the mockup's natural width, an `area` from its lowest shape. Returns the height, or `null` when the shape isn't drawn. |
| `resize(name, { h?, w? })` | Sets a shape's height or width. A new width on an area widens every top-level area in its column, the areas that share the resized area's left edge. Areas nested inside them keep their width. Each shape to the right of the column moves right by as much as the column area beside it grew, so a shape beside a narrower area clears that area's new edge. A shape beside no column area moves by as much as the resized area grew. |
| `move(name, { x?, y? }, pause?)` | Moves a shape to a new position. A card's follow-up parts move with the card. An area moves with its shapes and its nested areas. The area the shape leaves and the area the shape lands in fit their height again. Move shapes with `move` rather than through `editor.updateShape`, which leaves parts behind and fits no area. |
| `flow(area, names, { top?, gap? })` | Lays the named shapes out one under another inside an area, from `top` (60 units under the area's top edge by default) with `gap` between them (30 by default). The area grows to hold them before they move, so no shape lands past the area's bottom edge, where the next area down would take the shape. |
| `classificationTree(name, spec, { x, y })` | Draws one test branch whole, in one batch, as an `area` labelled `spec.label`: the root as a blue box, each classification as a violet box joined to the root by a line with no arrowheads, each partition as a green box joined the same way, and the matrix under them. A matrix row has a narrow `★` column on the far left (`★` when `isNew: true`, blank otherwise), its id and summary next to it, a filled dot under each partition it picks, and its expected outcome, kind and setup on the right. A row with `manual: true` is orange. Grey dotted lines run between the rows, after the `★` column, and down each partition's column; the dropped rows (`Dropped: …`), deleted tests (`Deleted: …`) and the note sit in grey below the matrix when present. `spec` holds `label`, `root`, `classifications` (each a `name` and its `partitions` as `[key, label]` pairs), `rows` (each `id`, `summary`, `picks` as one partition key per classification, `expected`, `kind`, `setup?`, `manual?` and `isNew?`), `dropped?`, `deleted?` and `note?`. With a name that exists, draws the branch again in place under fresh ids. |

For example, a question with its follow-up in an open area:

```js
await canvas.card('q4', { x, y, w: 1160, text: '❓ Q4 · <title>\n\n<body>' })
await canvas.followUp('q4', { summary: 'Summary · Q4 so far\n\n<settled and findings>', note: '<how the answer was read>' })
await canvas.note('n2', { text: '<the next reading>' })
```

A session that needs more than these writes its own helpers as scripts in the canvas folder, loads them into the tab, and loads them again after a relaunch.

## Mockups

Mockups import the shared pieces from `@canvas/kit`: `theme`, with the ink, paper, colours, hand font and a sketched border, and `Browser`, a browser window around a screen. Five kinds are built in: `cylinder`, whose data is `{ title, caption }`; `area`, a rounded dashed region whose data is `{ label, isFocus }`, which draws a solid red border while focused, for grouping the shapes inside a part, used instead of a frame and sent to the back; `mermaid`, whose data is `{ source }`, a mermaid diagram drawn in the canvas's ink and hand font; `code-snippet`, a fragment of code or config; and `blank-screen`. Use a `mermaid` shape for a finished diagram that will change little. Draw an exploration or an unsettled diagram with tldraw shapes, which are easier to change. A `mermaid` shape scales its diagram to fit and keeps the diagram's proportions. Create it with `mermaid(name, …)`, which sizes it to the diagram. Write and validate the source with superpowers:mermaid. The shape draws with pele, the renderer superpowers:mermaid's PNG comes from, so it looks like that PNG.

Use a `code-snippet` to show a change to a file, such as a config the user has not seen. Its data is `{ file, tag, lines, gutterNotes, highlight, view, expanded }`. Each line is `{ text, mark, note }`, where `mark` is `same`, `add`, `remove` or `gap`, and a `gap` line draws `⋯` for the code left out. With `gutterNotes`, each line's `note` sits beside it, starting at the line's height without making the line taller. A note longer than two lines shows its first two lines and a "more…" link that expands it. `highlight` is a list of `{ pattern, color }` rules that the snippet tries in order at each position of a line. It defaults to JS/TS; pass rules for another language. `view` is `unified`, with `+` and `−` marks, or `split`, with the old code on the left and the new on the right. A toggle in the header switches between the two views. `view` is `code` for a file shown as it is rather than as a change. In that view the snippet has no toggle, no `+` and `−` marks and no mark colours, only the code with its highlighting.

Keep them low fidelity: the hand font, sketched borders, and grey bars for text that does not matter.

When the screen has a prototype, copy the mockup from it: the same parts, the same states and the same copy, translated into the language the canvas is written in. A state that is its own view in the prototype is its own mockup on the canvas.

- **Size a mock to its content** when the content's height depends on its data. Give the mockup's root element a `data-root` attribute, and lay it out from the top with no bottom edge. Zoom your tab to the shape, and once the shape has rendered, set the shape's `h` to the root's `offsetHeight` times the shape's width over the mockup's natural width. The canvas renders only the shapes on screen, so a shape measured off screen has no root element. Its `h` then drops to a few units while its content still draws at full size, and every arrow bound to the shape ends at its top edge. `fit(name)` does all of this, and `mock(name, …)` calls it after creating the shape.
- **Make a mockup interactive** when the user needs to switch what it shows, such as a view or a collapsed part. Mark each element that takes a click with `data-interactive`; tldraw keeps every other click for selecting and moving the shape. `render` receives `update(patch)` as its second argument, which merges the patch into the shape's `data`, so the canvas saves the change and every tab shows it. While the shape is on screen, the canvas keeps the shape's height equal to the height of its `data-root` element, so a click that grows or shrinks the content resizes the shape.
- **A shape's `data` holds only JSON.** An `undefined` anywhere inside it fails validation and crashes every open tab; write `null` instead.

## Drawing

- **Notes are free text.** A short sentence with an arrow to the spot it describes. Never a sticky note, since sticky notes are the user's messages.
- **Arrows point at an element's centre**, so they follow when the element moves. An arrow points at a specific spot only when it means that spot: a button, an option, a row.
- **To point at a spot inside a mock**, such as one card in a mockup that draws several, give that element an attribute that names it. Read the element's bounds in the page, convert its corner or edge to a page point with `editor.screenToPage`, and bind the arrow's end to the mock with that point as a `normalizedAnchor`, `isPrecise: true` and `isExact: true`. Without `isExact` the arrow stops at the mock's outer edge.
- Text is black, arrow labels included, and written in tldraw's default font, the hand font (`font: 'draw'`): prose, notes, labels and cards alike. Use the monospace font only where the loading skill asks for it, such as a tree of leaves.
- **Draw each kind of part with its own shape.** Draw each of the system's own modules as a rectangle, coloured by the deployable it belongs to. Draw a store as a cylinder, titled with the product that holds the data, such as `<provider> Postgres`, and captioned with the data it holds. Draw an external service as a cloud, the client as an ellipse, and a platform or a deployable as an `area` around its parts.
- **Label each arrow with the payload or the action it carries**, and with the binding, protocol or credential it goes through when that matters.
- **Spread the canvas across columns instead of letting it grow downwards.** Put related parts in the same column, and start a new column to the right for a part unrelated to the existing ones. Give all top-level areas in a column the same width.
- **Lay a flow out left to right.** Put whoever starts it on the left, stores in a column of their own next to the modules that write them, and external services along the far edge. Draw a process as a vertical column of numbered steps, each with the store or service it reaches on the same row, so its arrow runs straight across.
- **Leave room under a title.** Keep the first shape inside an area clear of the area's label.
- **Keep every shape, label and arrow clear of the others.** When a straight arrow would cross a shape or another arrow's label, curve it with `bend` or move its label with `labelPosition`. When labels crowd each other, move the shapes apart.
- **Leave room for each arrow's label.** Place two shapes joined by a labelled arrow 250 to 300 units apart. With a gap of about 100, the label wraps one word per line over the arrow and the shapes. Keep a label to a few words, since it wraps to the width of its gap. Lay the shapes out with these gaps before drawing the first arrow, instead of fixing collisions after the screenshot.
- **When notes around one diagram would send arrows across it**, centre the diagram and place each note on the side nearest the element it points at, stacked in the same order as their targets so no two arrows cross. When arrows or notes still overlap, add space between the elements or above them and move the notes there.
- **Box the parts of one thing with an `area`, never a frame.** When several separate shapes are parts of the same thing, such as the variants of one part or the screens of one sequence, draw a `mock` shape of kind `area` around them. Send it to the back. Shapes that only sit near each other get no area.
- **Resize an area whenever what it holds grows or moves**, so it keeps a margin around its contents.
- **Set `growY: 0` whenever a script sets a geo shape's `h`.** tldraw keeps the `growY` it computed for the earlier size, and the shape stays taller than what it holds. To stack shapes inside a geo shape under its label, read the label's height first: the height of the shape's `.tl-rich-text` element divided by the zoom level.
- **Delete the arrows of the shapes you delete.** An arrow bound to a deleted shape stays on the canvas where it was drawn. After deleting shapes, delete every arrow with fewer than two bindings.
- **Group what moves together.** Each element, or each set of elements that belong together, is one tldraw group with its title, made with `editor.groupShapes`. Group no further than the smallest set that is one cohesive thing. Elements joined by arrows can share a group, such as the steps of one flow. An element that stands on its own gets its own group, even when an arrow joins it to another element. Arrows between two groups stay outside both, so they stay attached at each end when either group moves.

## Working with the user

- **Your tab holds the current state.** Read what you change from `window.editor` right before changing it, since the user may have moved it. Once the user has edited the canvas, never rebuild it; change only the shapes the change touches.
- **Focus the area you are drawing in.** The focused area draws a solid red border instead of the grey dashed one, so the user can follow where your actions are happening. Pass `focus: true` when creating an area you are about to fill, and call `focus(name)` on the existing area when the work moves there. Leave the focus alone for a small adjustment to one shape: change it only when an area becomes where you will draw for a while, and clear it with `focus(null)` when you stop drawing.
- **Talking in the chat.** Say what changed and ask in the reply. The user answers in the chat, by voice, or with sticky notes.
- **Talking on the canvas.** Write what you would say in the chat as an Agent note, a grey dashed rectangle labelled `Agent`, in the part of the canvas it is about. The user answers with sticky notes or by voice. The loading skill says which of the two to use; when it does not, ask the user.
- **Never reuse a deleted shape's id.** Sync sends a deleted shape recreated under its id as an update to the old record, so a new shape of another type under that id fails validation in every open tab.
- **A sticky note on the canvas is a message from the user.** When you give the user the URL, tell them to put a sticky note on the shape they want changed, or to draw an arrow from the note to it. `window.canvas.notes()` returns each note with its targets: the shapes an arrow joins it to, else the shapes it sits on, smallest first. Act on each note, and once it is handled, delete it together with its `arrows` and tell the user.
- **"Send to Agent", or Ctrl+, (Cmd+, on a Mac), notifies that a batch of edits is ready.** The document is already saved. While the canvas is open, keep `canvas.sh watch` running under a monitor that notifies you on every line it prints; each line is a click. A background command that reports only when it exits never tells you about a click, and you never read the user's notes. Do not react to the user's edits between clicks. When the monitor expires, start it again.
- **The mic button, or holding Ctrl+. (Cmd+. on a Mac), sends a voice message.** The user holds it while talking and releases it to send; the browser's speech recognition turns the speech into text, in the browser's language unless the URL carries `?lang=<code>`. The watch prints it as `voice: <message>`, followed by ` | selected: <id> (<type>: "<text>"), …` when the user had shapes selected as they released it, and the document is saved first, as with a click. The selected shapes are what the message's "this" or "here" refers to. Treat it as a message from the user in the chat: answer it, and read the canvas for any notes it refers to. A notification can cut a long voice message short. When a message reads as cut off, read its whole line in the watch monitor's output file before acting on it.

## Export

1. **Unslop the texts.** Collect the output of `canvas.sh texts` and the explanatory texts written inside the mockups the document uses into a file in the change's scratch folder, and run superpowers:unslop over it. When that skill is not installed, say so and continue. Apply the findings that survive verification to the canvas and the mockups.
2. **Export.** Run `canvas.sh export`. The loading skill places the SVG where it needs the image.

## Ending

When the loading skill's work is done, or the user moves on to other work, stop the canvas: run `canvas.sh stop` on the document, stop the monitor running `canvas.sh watch`, and close your `agent-browser` tab.

## What this skill is not

It does not commit.

# Component tree on the canvas

`program-design`'s component tree reference still says what the part covers, what to read before proposing it and when it fits. The record keeps the text tree.

## Representation

One `component-cards` mock. Each component is a card inside the card of the component that renders it. Each tree root starts a column, and roots that belong together, such as the components that host the same element, share one.

- **Colour each card by the component's kind:** `host` for a component of the host app that only renders the new ones, `provider` for one that holds state and renders nothing of its own, `scope` for one that adds values for everything inside it, `dialog`, `view` for one of the views a parent switches between, `part` for a piece of a view, `button`, and `slot` for a place where the component that renders it puts its own content.
- **Tag each card with its repository and with whether the change adds the component, touches it, or leaves it unchanged.** A new card has a solid border, a touched card a dashed one, and an unchanged card a dotted grey one. Draw an unchanged card only when it renders a card the change adds or touches.
- **A card with `row`** lays its children side by side, for views that replace each other.
- **A slot is a `slot` card named `<slot>`**, inside the card of the component that exposes it. Where the branch defines the component, the slot card is empty. Where a screen uses the component, draw the component as unchanged and put inside each slot card the cards that screen fills it with.
- **The legend under the cards** lists every colour.

Explain each card with a free-text note beside the diagram, with an arrow pointing at the card's title. In the note, write what the component renders, what state it owns and why it exists rather than staying inline. A component rendered in more than one place gets its notes on one instance, and the other instance gets one note saying it has the same cards. Point each arrow at a spot inside the mock as `canvas` describes, finding the card by its `data-card` attribute, which holds the card's name.

**Centre the mock in its area, with notes on both sides.** Put each note on the side nearest the card it explains: a note on the left points at the card's left edge, and a note on the right at its right edge. Stack each side's notes in the order of their cards, so no arrow crosses a card or another arrow. Before showing the part, check the screenshot for an arrow that crosses a card. When an arrow crosses a card, move the note that the arrow starts from to the other side.

## Example

```js
{
  kind: 'component-cards',
  data: {
    columns: [
      [{ name: '<Providers>', kind: 'host', repo: '<app>', change: 'touched', children: [
        { name: '<Provider>', kind: 'provider', repo: '<library>', change: 'new', children: [
          { name: '<Dialog>', kind: 'dialog', repo: '<library>', change: 'new', row: true, children: [
            { name: '<Form>', kind: 'view', repo: '<library>', change: 'new' },
            { name: '<Done>', kind: 'view', repo: '<library>', change: 'new' },
          ] },
        ] },
      ] }],
      [{ name: '<Host>', kind: 'host', repo: '<app>', change: 'touched', children: [
        { name: '<Trigger>', kind: 'button', repo: '<library>', change: 'new' },
      ] }],
    ],
  },
}
```

# State on the canvas

`program-design`'s derivation ledger reference still says what the part covers, what to read before proposing it and when it fits. The record keeps the text ledger.

## Representation

One `state-card` mock per component, in the same columns as the component tree, and one `hook-card` mock per hook or function the branch adds. Size each card to its content as `canvas` describes.

- **A line is `name := expression`**, with a comment under it when the reader needs something the expression leaves out, and a tag on the right from `program-design`'s derivation ledger. Draw each tag in the colour of its kind, and give tags of a similar kind similar colours:

  | Kind | Tags and colours |
  |---|---|
  | What the part receives, greens | `prop` `#0ca678`, `arg` `#20c997`, `request` `#2b8a3e` |
  | Configuration, olives | `query meta` `#5c940d`, `env` `#74b816`, `config` `#66a80f` |
  | Shared state from above | `context` `#7048e8`, `cookie` `#c2255c` |
  | Read from outside, blues and orange | `server` `#1c7ed6`, `upstream` `#1971c2`, `database` `#364fc7`, `browser` `#e8590c` |
  | Held by the part, greys and amber | `local` `#495057`, `constant` `#5c677d`, `form` `#f08c00` |
  | Functions, teals | `function` `#0b7285`, `method` `#1098ad`, `effect` `#15aabf` |
  | Derived | `computed` `#868e96` |
  | Last line | `returns` `#212529` |

  When a branch adds a tag to the ledger, give the tag a colour from its kind's family that differs from the other colours in that family.
- **Lines go in the order they appear in the code:** props first, then context, query meta and cookies, then local and form state, then server queries and mutations, then browser reads, then computed values. A value comes before any line that uses it.
- **Only add variables when necessary.** If a value is used once, inline it where it is used, in the `returns` line or in an argument. Hooks and functions build the return value directly on the `return`, never step by step or through separate variables. Components do the same in the JSX: a value the JSX can use directly goes there instead of in a separate variable, such as a field destructured from a query's data.
- **The last line says what the component renders or what the hook returns**, tagged `returns`, with no name and no `:=`, in the same style as the other lines. For a component, write it as a tree of the elements the component renders, never as code, JSX or prose: one element per line, `├─` and `└─` before its children, and `←` before the props the element passes, each as a name or as `<prop> ← <where its value comes from>`. A condition goes on its own line under the element it shows or hides. Put the conditions of what renders in this line, never in a computed value that only feeds it. The card draws `⇒` in the name column of that line and a dashed rule above that line, so the reader can tell the returns line from the lines above it.
- **A hook card** starts with what the hook does in one line, then its arguments, what it reads, what it computes and what it returns.

**Join the cards with arrows before showing the part**, so the reader can follow each value from where it is made to where it is used. For example:

- From a component card to a card it renders, labelled with what crosses between them, such as `renders · <props>` or a callback with its arguments.
- From a provider's card to a card that reads its context, such as `context · <the values that card reads>`.
- From a hook or a function to its caller, as a grey dashed arrow with no label. Place the hook card next to its caller's card.

Leave room between the columns for the labels, and curve an arrow around a column's side when a straight one would cross a card.

Write each proposal and each point that the design leaves unsettled as a free-text note next to the card the note is about.

## Example

```js
{
  kind: 'state-card',
  data: {
    title: '<Trigger>', kind: 'button', repo: '<library>',
    lines: [
      ['<configurationId>', '"<configuration>"', 'prop', 'set by <Host>'],
      ['<buttonProps>', 'every other prop', 'prop', 'passed straight to Button'],
      ['<start>', 'use<Start>({ <configurationId> })', 'context', 'null without a provider'],
      ['returns', 'nothing while <start> is missing; otherwise\nButton ← ...<buttonProps>, onClick: <start>', 'returns', null],
    ],
  },
}
```

```js
{
  kind: 'hook-card',
  data: {
    name: 'use<Start>', kind: 'hook', repo: '<library>',
    does: 'builds the callback a trigger calls to start',
    lines: [
      ['<configurationId>', 'argument', 'arg'],
      ['<provider>', 'use<Context>()', 'context'],
      ['returns', '<provider> == null ? null : a callback that starts with <configurationId>', 'returns'],
    ],
  },
}
```

Never leave a line's source empty, and never put `undefined` in `data`; write `null` for a missing comment.

# Interfaces on the canvas

`program-design`'s interfaces reference still says what the part covers, what to read before proposing it and when it fits. The record keeps the JSON Schemas.

## Representation

One diagram of `interface-card` mocks joined by arrows.

- **Give each repository its own column inside an `area`.** Label the area with the repository, and add the package name when the repository holds several packages. Inside a repository, put each kind of part in its own column, side by side and with no header: components first, then hooks and functions. Align a card with the card that renders or calls it when the column leaves room.
- **Draw each part as an `interface-card`.** Its `kind` sets the shape: a `component` has square corners, a `hook` is a pill, a `function` has a double border, an `endpoint` is a hexagon and a `type` has rounded corners. Its `change` sets the colour: `new` is green, `touched` amber and dashed, `pending` blue and dotted for an endpoint another root settles, and `shared` violet for a type.
- **List the part's inputs on the card, one member per line, and its return value under the rule.** Write "no arguments" on a part with no inputs, and "props unchanged" on a host component whose props do not change. Leave the path off the card, because the file tree holds the paths.
- **Put each type under the part that uses it first**, in the same column, joined to that part by a violet dotted arrow labelled `uses`, `returns` or `sends`. When several cards share the types, such as the views of one dialog, put the types under the last of those cards.
- **Label each arrow with the props, arguments or request it carries**: `renders · <props>`, `calls · <arguments>`, `GET`, `POST`, or the callback a hook hands back. Run an arrow between two columns from the facing edge of one card to the facing edge of the other. When an arrow inside one column would cross a card, curve it around the column's left side. Keep every arrow and label clear of the cards.
- **The legend under the diagram** lists every shape and colour.

## Example

```js
{ kind: 'interface-card', data: { name: '<ResourceTrigger>', kind: 'component', change: 'new', repo: '<library>', inputs: [['<resourceName>', 'string'], ['<entityId>?', 'string'], ['...buttonProps', 'ButtonProps']] } }
{ kind: 'interface-card', data: { name: '<useResourceAction>', kind: 'hook', change: 'new', repo: '<library>', inputs: [['<resourceName>', 'string']], output: '(() => void) | null' } }
{ kind: 'interface-card', data: { name: 'GET /api/<resource>/{name}/', kind: 'endpoint', change: 'pending', repo: '<consumer-api>', inputs: [['name', 'string, in the path']], output: '<Resource>' } }
{ kind: 'interface-card', data: { name: '<Resource>', kind: 'type', change: 'shared', repo: '<library>', inputs: [['name', 'string'], ['labels', '{ [locale]: string }']] } }
```

import * as D1Client from "@effect/sql-d1/D1Client";
import { sql } from "drizzle-orm";
import * as SQLiteD1Drizzle from "drizzle-orm/effect-d1";
import type { EffectSQLiteD1Database } from "drizzle-orm/effect-d1";
import * as Context from "effect/Context";
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect";
import * as Layer from "effect/Layer";

export interface Statement {
  readonly toSQL: () => { readonly sql: string; readonly params: ReadonlyArray<unknown> };
}

// The Drizzle database over the D1 binding, plus the D1 client underneath it:
// Drizzle's effect-d1 driver has no batch, and D1 has no transactions, so writes
// that must land together go through the client's batch.
export class Database extends Context.Service<
  Database,
  {
    readonly db: EffectSQLiteD1Database;
    readonly client: D1Client.D1Client;
  }
>()("kurasu/Database") {
  static readonly layer = <E, R>(binding: Effect.Effect<D1Database, E, R>) =>
    Layer.unwrap(
      Effect.map(binding, (db) =>
        Layer.effect(
          Database,
          Effect.gen(function* () {
            const client = yield* D1Client.D1Client;

            const drizzle = yield* SQLiteD1Drizzle.makeWithDefaults({}).pipe(
              Effect.provideService(D1Client.D1Client, client),
            );

            return { db: drizzle, client };
          }),
        ).pipe(Layer.provide(D1Client.layer({ db }))),
      ),
    );
}

/** Runs Drizzle queries as one atomic D1 batch, in order. */
export const batch = (client: D1Client.D1Client, queries: ReadonlyArray<Statement>) =>
  client
    .batch(
      queries.map((query) => {
        const statement = query.toSQL();

        return client.unsafe(statement.sql, statement.params);
      }),
    )
    .pipe(Effect.orDie, Effect.asVoid);

export const firstRow =
  <Row, A>(decode: (row: Row) => Effect.Effect<A>) =>
  (rows: ReadonlyArray<Row>) => {
    const row = rows[0];

    return row == null ? Effect.succeedNone : Effect.asSome(decode(row));
  };

export const now = sql<Date>`(cast(unixepoch('subsec') * 1000 as integer))`;

servidor las conexiones al aula (shape 7) ``` ## 1 Qué se guarda La sesión suma dos campos, y la novedad un tipo. `featured` dice si la sesión es la destacada, y `featured_questions` si muestra sus preguntas en la card del inicio. Los dos son booleanos no nulos y valen falso en una sesión nueva. Cuando el cambio llega a producción, todas las sesiones tienen los dos en falso, así que no hay destacada hasta que el profe marca una. ```mermaid erDiagram SESSION ||--o{ CHANGELOG_ENTRY : "tiene novedades" SESSION { bool featured "no nulo, falso por defecto, único entre las sesiones sin borrar que lo tienen" bool featured_questions "no nulo, falso por defecto" } CHANGELOG_ENTRY { enum type "suma questions-opened" } ``` La base no deja que dos sesiones tengan `featured` en verdadero: un índice único parcial cubre solo las sesiones con `featured` en verdadero y sin borrar, igual que el índice que deja un solo código de registro vigente. La API desmarca la anterior en el mismo batch de D1 en el que marca la nueva, y la desmarca primero, porque el batch corre sus sentencias en orden y el índice rechazaría dos destacadas a la vez. Si una sentencia falla, D1 no aplica ninguna. La novedad suma el tipo `questions-opened`, que se muestra como "Preguntas abiertas" y apunta a la sesión. ## 2 Los estados Una sesión y sus preguntas destacadas tienen cada una su ciclo. ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 direction LR [*] --> Deshabilitada : el profe la crea Deshabilitada --> NoDestacada : habilitar, con Destacada apagado Deshabilitada --> Destacada : habilitar, con Destacada prendido Habilitada --> Deshabilitada : deshabilitar, con confirmación si es la destacada Deshabilitada --> [*] : el profe la borra state Habilitada { direction LR NoDestacada --> Destacada : el profe la destaca Destacada --> NoDestacada : le saca la marca, o destaca otra } NoDestacada : No destacada note right of Destacada : arriba en el inicio, con su aula abierta
y la única donde se vota y se pregunta classDef grey fill:#f3f4f6,stroke:#4b5563,color:#1f2937 classDef green fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,color:#1f2937 classDef blue fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb,color:#1f2937 class Deshabilitada grey class NoDestacada blue class Destacada green ``` Una sesión se crea deshabilitada. Habilitarla la lleva a habilitada, y dentro de habilitada está destacada o no destacada: habilitarla con el switch "Destacada" del modal prendido la lleva directo a destacada. Hay a lo sumo una destacada. Una sesión sale de destacada cuando el profe le saca la marca, cuando destaca otra o cuando la deshabilita, y las tres acciones piden confirmación porque cierran sus encuestas y bajan sus manos. Deshabilitar sale de habilitada desde cualquiera de sus dos estados. Solo se borra una deshabilitada. ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 direction TB [*] --> Cerradas : la sesión se crea Cerradas --> Abiertas : el profe las prende, solo en la destacada Abiertas --> Cerradas : el profe las apaga, o la sesión deja de ser la destacada note right of Abiertas : la card destacada del inicio muestra el panel de preguntas
y hay una novedad Preguntas abiertas pendiente note right of Cerradas : las preguntas se ven solo en el aula y en el modal classDef grey fill:#f3f4f6,stroke:#4b5563,color:#1f2937 classDef green fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,color:#1f2937 class Cerradas grey class Abiertas green ``` Las preguntas destacadas de una sesión están cerradas o abiertas. Arrancan cerradas, y el profe las abre y las cierra desde el panel del aula. Solo se abren en la destacada, y se cierran solas cuando la sesión deja de ser la destacada, así que en una sesión no destacada siempre están cerradas. ## 3 Cómo cambia la destacada ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber actor P as Profe participant W as Web del profe participant API as API participant DB as D1 participant Au as Aula de la anterior participant WE as Web de los estudiantes P->>W: Destaca la sesión, o la habilita con Destacada prendido W->>W: Pide confirmación si hay otra destacada W->>API: Un PATCH a la sesión con featured, y enabled si la habilita API->>API: Controla que la sesión quede habilitada alt Hay otra destacada API->>DB: Batch: desmarca la anterior, apaga sus preguntas destacadas, cierra sus encuestas activas, baja sus manos y marca la nueva API->>DB: Saca las novedades de la anterior: Preguntas abiertas y la de cada encuesta cerrada API->>Au: Aviso session Au-->>WE: Aviso a los conectados WE->>WE: Lleva al inicio a quien estaba en el aula else No hay otra API->>DB: Marca la nueva end API-->>W: La sesión W->>API: Vuelve a pedir las sesiones ``` El profe destaca una sesión con el switch "Destacada" o la habilita con ese switch prendido (1). Si hay otra destacada, la web pide confirmación y dice cuántas encuestas se cierran y cuántas manos se bajan (2). La web manda un solo pedido a la sesión, con `featured` y, si la está habilitando, `enabled` (3). La API controla que la sesión quede habilitada (4). Si había otra destacada, escribe en un batch: desmarca la anterior, le apaga las preguntas destacadas, cierra sus encuestas activas, baja sus manos y, al final, marca la nueva (5). Después saca las novedades de la anterior: "Preguntas abiertas" y la de cada encuesta que cerró (6). Avisa al aula de la anterior con "session" (7, 8), y la web lleva al inicio a quien estaba en ella (9). La respuesta vuelve a la web del profe (11), que pide de nuevo las sesiones (12). Para la confirmación, la web del profe toma la destacada de la lista de sesiones del admin, que trae `featured`, pide sus encuestas y sus manos con los mismos pedidos que usa la página de esa sesión, y cuenta las encuestas activas y las manos. Cuando el profe habilita una sesión con "Destacada" prendido y hay otra destacada, el aviso del modal es la confirmación, y no hay otro paso. Si el pedido falla, el error aparece dentro del diálogo, que queda abierto. Sacarle la marca a la destacada y deshabilitarla siguen el mismo camino sin la sesión nueva: el batch desmarca, apaga, cierra y baja, y el resto es igual. Las novedades corren después del batch, como hoy: si sacarlas falla, el cambio queda guardado y la API registra la falla en su log. El inicio del estudiante no recibe avisos, así que ve la nueva destacada cuando la web vuelve a pedir las sesiones, cada cinco minutos o al recargar. ## 4 Cómo llegan las preguntas a la card ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber actor P as Profe participant W as Web del profe participant API as API participant DB as D1 participant WE as Web del estudiante actor E as Estudiante P->>W: Prende las preguntas destacadas en el aula W->>API: PATCH a la sesión con featured_questions alt La sesión es la destacada API->>DB: Guarda featured_questions API->>DB: Crea la novedad Preguntas abiertas API-->>W: La sesión else No es la destacada API-->>W: Rechaza end Note over WE: Hasta cinco minutos después, o al recargar WE->>API: Pide las sesiones API-->>WE: Sesiones, con featured y featured_questions WE->>API: Pide las preguntas de la destacada WE-->>E: La card con el panel de preguntas ``` El profe prende las preguntas destacadas en el panel del aula (1), y la web lo manda en el mismo pedido a la sesión que usa el resto de sus ajustes (2). Si la sesión es la destacada, la API guarda el ajuste y crea la novedad "Preguntas abiertas" (3 a 5); si no, lo rechaza (6). Apagarlo sigue el mismo camino y saca la novedad. Del lado del estudiante, la lista de sesiones trae `featured` y `featured_questions` (8, 9), y la web deja de calcular la destacada por su cuenta: la toma de `featured`, en el inicio y en el aula. Con `featured_questions` prendido, la card pide las preguntas de la destacada (10), con el mismo pedido que usan el modal y el aula, y muestra el panel (11). Preguntar, votar y borrar desde la card usan los mismos pedidos que el aula, y después de cada uno la web vuelve a pedir la lista. En el inicio, la web pide las encuestas activas con el id de la destacada, en vez de pedir las de todas las sesiones y filtrarlas. ## 5 Las reglas de la API ### Escrituras del estudiante ```mermaid flowchart TD S["Escritura del estudiante: votar una encuesta, preguntar, votar o borrar una pregunta, levantar o bajar la mano"] --> V{"Sesión habilitada y no borrada?"} V -->|No| X((Rechazada)) V -->|Sí| F{"Es la destacada?"} F -->|No| X F -->|Sí| R["Reglas propias de cada acción"] R --> G((Guardada)) classDef step fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,color:#1f2937 classDef dec fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb,color:#1f2937 classDef bad fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#dc2626,color:#1f2937 classDef ok fill:#ffedd5,stroke:#ea580c,color:#1f2937 class S,R step class V,F dec class X bad class G ok ``` Toda escritura del estudiante sobre una sesión pasa dos controles antes que los propios de la acción: que la sesión esté habilitada y no borrada, y que sea la destacada. Son votar una encuesta, preguntar, votar o borrar una pregunta, y levantar o bajar la mano. ### Escrituras del profe en la destacada ```mermaid flowchart TD T["Escritura del profe: activar una encuesta o prender las preguntas destacadas"] --> F{"Es la destacada?"} F -->|No| X((Rechazada)) F -->|Sí| G((Guardada)) classDef step fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,color:#1f2937 classDef dec fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb,color:#1f2937 classDef bad fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#dc2626,color:#1f2937 classDef ok fill:#ffedd5,stroke:#ea580c,color:#1f2937 class T step class F dec class X bad class G ok ``` Las escrituras del profe que solo tienen sentido en la destacada, activar una encuesta y prender las preguntas destacadas, pasan el control de la destacada. ### Destacar una sesión ```mermaid flowchart TD D["Destacar una sesión"] --> E{"Está habilitada, o se habilita en el mismo pedido?"} E -->|No| X((Rechazada)) E -->|Sí| G((Guardada, junto con la salida de la anterior)) classDef step fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,color:#1f2937 classDef dec fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb,color:#1f2937 classDef bad fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#dc2626,color:#1f2937 classDef ok fill:#ffedd5,stroke:#ea580c,color:#1f2937 class D step class E dec class X bad class G ok ``` Destacar una sesión exige que esté habilitada o que se habilite en el mismo pedido, y se guarda junto con la salida de la destacada anterior (rama 3). Sin destacada, nadie entra a ningún aula, porque el control de entrada no encuentra sesión destacada. La web hace los mismos controles antes de mandar el pedido: no muestra Activar fuera de la destacada, deshabilita el switch de preguntas destacadas y no deja votar ni preguntar fuera de la card destacada. La API manda. Un rechazo no guarda nada, y la web lo muestra como cualquier error de una acción. ## 6 Las novedades ```mermaid flowchart LR C{"Cambio"} -->|"prender las preguntas destacadas"| A["Crea Preguntas abiertas"] C -->|"activar una encuesta"| B["Crea Encuesta abierta"] C -->|"apagar las preguntas destacadas, también al dejar de ser la destacada"| R1["Saca Preguntas abiertas"] C -->|"cerrar o borrar una encuesta, también al dejar de ser la destacada"| R2["Saca Encuesta abierta"] C -->|"primera pregunta, primera respuesta, destacar la sesión"| N((Nada)) A --> P(("Pendiente hasta que el profe la anuncia o la descarta")) B --> P classDef dec fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#2563eb,color:#1f2937 classDef make fill:#ffedd5,stroke:#ea580c,color:#1f2937 classDef drop fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#dc2626,color:#1f2937 classDef none fill:#f3f4f6,stroke:#4b5563,color:#1f2937 class C dec class A,B make class R1,R2 drop class N,P none ``` Prender las preguntas destacadas crea la novedad "Preguntas abiertas" en la sesión, y apagarlas la saca, también cuando se apagan porque la sesión deja de ser la destacada. Activar una encuesta crea "Encuesta abierta", y cerrarla o borrarla la saca, también cuando se cierra por lo mismo. Las dos quedan pendientes hasta que el profe las anuncia o las descarta. Ni la primera respuesta de una encuesta ni la primera pregunta sacan su novedad, y destacar una sesión no crea ninguna. El link del anuncio usa la marca: lleva a la home cuando la sesión anunciada es la destacada al enviar, y a la home con `?sesion=` cuando no lo es. ## 7 Las pantallas Los prototipos son la representación de esta rama. `prototypes/card-preguntas.html` muestra el inicio del estudiante. Con las preguntas destacadas prendidas, la card destacada tiene el panel de preguntas arriba de las encuestas activas: el campo para preguntar, las tres más votadas y las propias, y "Mostrar N preguntas más". # kurasu: architecture rules

verified: 2026-10-19

Answers how kurasu's backend code is split and which rules its Effect code follows.

## Knowledge

- `packages/core` defines services named after a job (sessions, polls, access, mailer) and their ports. It imports no adapter and nothing from Cloudflare, Alchemy, Drizzle or jose.
- Adapters live outside core: the D1 adapters in `packages/database`, the R2, Email Sending, JWT and Durable Object adapters in `apps/api`. The apps wire the core services to their adapters; packages never import apps.
- Expected failures are typed errors declared with Schema; the code does not catch defects as if they were expected.
- Decode everything that enters at a boundary (a request body, a stored row, a message) with its schema before using it.
- The Worker reads configuration with Effect `Config` where it is built and passes it to the layers as plain values (`Access.layer(webOrigin)`, `JoseSessionTokens(jwtSecret)`). Secrets come from varlock: `.env.schema` declares them and `.env.local`, out of git, holds them. The mail binding and the D1 resource also read two test-only variables, `KURASU_MAIL_ALLOWED_DESTINATIONS` and `KURASU_D1_IMPORT_FILES`, which `.env.schema` declares without a default, so `Config.option` reads them as absent outside the API tests.
- Declare Alchemy resources outside the Worker's runtime path, because a Worker's initialization runs once at deploy and again when the isolate starts. The API Worker builds its HTTP app, with every layer that reads D1, inside `fetch`, because the bindings exist only when the isolate starts (see `alchemy/local-dev`).
- Reads are bounded (a list has a maximum) and paginate by key, not by offset.
- D1 has no transactions: writes that must land together go in one batch.

## Sources

- `.scratch/aula-virtual/program-design/kurasu.md`, branches 1 to 4 and Standards.
- `app/apps/api/src/worker.ts`.
# kurasu: API shape

verified: 2026-10-19

Answers how kurasu's HTTP API is laid out: what is a route, what is a filter, and what travels inside a resource.

## Knowledge

- Each resource has one endpoint, never nested: `/api/<resource>` and `/api/<resource>/{id}`. The one exception is a resource's binary content, at `/{id}/file` (`GET /api/materials/{id}/file`).
- The student uses `/api/<resource>` and the teacher `/api/admin/<resource>`; each side gets only the operations it needs.
- The id of another resource goes in as a filter (`?sessionId=`) or in the body, never in the path.
- A resource includes the values that belong to it: the student's vote is a field of the poll (`myResponse`) and of the question (`myVote`), set with a `PATCH` on that resource.
- A list returns a summary and the detail returns the full resource (`SessionSummary` and `Session`).
- Actions that are not resources, such as requesting a login link or opening a session, stay as actions under `/api/auth/`.
- A malformed teacher request answers a typed 400 and stores nothing: `InvalidPollContent` for poll content of another type (options outside `choice`, scale labels outside `scale`) and `InvalidUpload` for a multipart upload whose fields come after the file or do not decode. Changing the access of a user id that does not exist answers `UserNotFound` (404).
- Every endpoint behind the login also answers the access middleware's errors (requesting a link and opening a session have no middleware): `Unauthenticated`, `NoAccess`, and `NotTeacher` on `/api/admin`.

## Sources

- `.scratch/aula-virtual/program-design/kurasu.md`, branches 3 and 4.

# kurasu: web rules

verified: 2026-10-22

Answers how kurasu's web is built: how screens share pieces, how they reach the API and where files go.

## Knowledge

- A piece used by both the student and the teacher is one component. The common part is inside it, and what each side adds enters through slots: a `ReactNode` prop for a fixed place, or a function that receives the row (`renderActions`, `renderHand`) for a per-row place. There is no admin flag.
- In program designs, slots follow the notation of the plugin's `component-tree` reference: `<slot>`.
- API access follows the wiki entry `tanstack-query/operation-hooks`: one hook per operation in `apps/web/src/features/<topic>/<hook>.ts`, keys from `queryKeys`, and typed `options` passed through. Each operation hook is built on `useApiQuery` or `useApiMutation` (`apps/web/src/api/`), which call `runApi` with the Effect HttpApi client. A screen never calls `useQuery` or `useMutation` directly. A query whose `queryOptions` are shared with a non-hook caller calls `useQuery` over those options instead: `useMaterialFile` (shared with the slides check).
- An operation hook does not list its errors by hand. Its `options` take `EndpointError<"group", "endpoint">` (`apps/web/src/api/api-error.ts`), which reads the error type of that endpoint from the HttpApi client: the endpoint's own errors, its middleware's (`Unauthenticated`, `NoAccess`, `NotTeacher`), `HttpClientError` and `SchemaError`. `useApiQuery` and `useApiMutation` infer the error type from `call` too, so options that name another endpoint's errors fail to typecheck. An endpoint without the login middleware, such as `auth.requestLink`, has no `Unauthenticated` in its errors.
- `useApiMutation` runs the hook's own callbacks before the screen's, and invalidates its `invalidates` keys before the screen's `onSuccess`, so the screen always sees fresh data.
- An instant action passes `optimistic` to `useApiMutation`: a list of entries built with `optimisticPatch({ key, exact?, patch })` (`api/optimistic-patch.ts`). `key` is a function of the input, because some keys name one record, such as one session. `exact` is for a key that is a prefix of other keys holding another data type. The mutation cancels and snapshots those keys, patches them before the request, puts the snapshot back on failure and invalidates after a failure too.
- A mutation's `errorToast` is a function of the input that returns the toast text, or `undefined` for no toast (a word cloud vote shows its error inline instead). An access error shows no toast; the query client sends the user to the login instead.
- The toast comes from sonner. `<Toaster>` is mounted in `__root`, and `showError(text)` and `showSuccess(text)` in `ui/toast.ts` call `toast.custom` with the shared `ui/Toast`, whose `variant` sets the icon and the role: `error` is an alert with the danger icon, `success` a status with the check. They are plain functions so a hook's `onError` or `onSuccess` can call them. `test/setup.ts` calls `toast.dismiss()` after each test, because sonner keeps its toasts in module state outside the rendered tree and one test's toast would show up in the next.
- Loading: a part that reads data renders `data == null ? <SkeletonOf>…</SkeletonOf> : …`. `ui/SkeletonOf` wraps the real part filled with example data, kept per topic in `features/<topic>/*-examples.ts`, so the skeleton takes the part's own size. Skeletons are coarse: wrap a whole card (the highlighted session, each card of a folding section, each poll card, each list row, the slide, the header's name and avatar), never the inside of one. `.skeleton` paints the wrapped card as one soft grey block in the theme's colours and hides everything inside it, text, buttons and icons included. It adds the `.skeleton` class, `inert` and `aria-hidden`. It adds `aria-hidden` as well as `inert` because Testing Library ignores `inert`, and a screen reader must not read the example data.
- The login check does not block the page. `useMe` is built on `useApiQuery`, and components do the redirects: `_app` renders `<Navigate to="/setup">` for an incomplete profile, and the query client sends the user to the login on an access error.
- A query throws to the error boundary only when it has no data and the error is not an access error (`throwOnError` in `api/create-query-client.ts`); a failed refetch keeps the data already on screen. The router's `defaultErrorComponent` is `ui/ErrorScreen`, whose "Volver al inicio" calls `queryClient.resetQueries` on the queries in error before navigating home. Resetting React Query's error boundary is not enough: the reset lasts only until the first query mounts, so a page reached through a redirect, such as the teacher's `/admin` after `/`, mounts its query still in error and throws again.
- A query that only one role may run waits for the role with `enabled`. The API answers the other role with a 403, `NotStudent` or `NotTeacher`, which is not an access error. When the screen has no data yet, `throwOnError` sends that 403 to the error screen. On `/`, the student's sessions and active polls pass `enabled: me.data?.role === "student"`, so they wait for `me`, and the page draws the student's skeleton meanwhile.
- `ui/Button` is the only text button, with variants `main`, `pill`, `pill-dark` and `pill-danger`, and a `pending` prop with an optional `pendingLabel`. A pending button is disabled, shows a spinner and keeps its full colour. `Button` renders only a `<button>`. A link styled as a button is `ui/ButtonLink`, with the same variants and `to`/`params` typed per route as in the router's `Link`. `ButtonLink` renders the router's `Link`, so it navigates inside the app. Icon buttons (`icon-button`) stay outside both.
- The upload dialog and the material list check an HTML marked as slides with the same `useSlidesCheck` (`features/materials/`), and show its state with `SlidesCheckNotice`. The hook loads the HTML in a hidden `SlidesFrame` that the caller renders from `frame`. It shows the result no earlier than one second after `start`, so a fast check does not show and hide its notice at once. The list passes `okFor: 10_000`, so its ok notice goes away after 10 s; the dialog passes no `okFor`, so its ok notice has no time limit.
- `useClassroom` handles live classroom updates. Each WebSocket notice invalidates the keys of its topic, and data always comes through the hooks.
- Confirmations and overlays use the shared pieces in `ui/`. `ConfirmAction` holds the dialog's state (closed, asking, confirming, failed), takes a `renderTrigger`, an `onConfirm` and an `errorText`, and wraps `ConfirmDialog`. The dialog closes when `onConfirm` resolves and stays open with `errorText` when `onConfirm` rejects. `ConfirmDialog` takes `pending`, `pendingLabel` and `error`; while pending, Cancelar is disabled and neither Escape nor a click outside closes it. `Backdrop` draws the background of a sheet, an alert or the projected view, and closes on a click outside its content and on Escape.
- Escape closes only the topmost open backdrop. `useCloseOnEscape` keeps one shared stack of closers and one `keydown` listener; with one listener per backdrop, Escape would also close the sheet under a confirmation. The browser runs microtasks between listeners, so by the time the sheet's listener runs, the confirmation is gone and the sheet is on top.
- Folders follow the topic, not the file kind: `features/<topic>/` holds a topic's components and hooks together. Browser state helpers go in `helpers/` (`helpers/local-ui/`), shared UI in `ui/`.
- Each file holds one component or hook, and uses named exports.
- Styles use Tailwind 4; the prototypes' colours and dark mode live in the theme.
- Repeated styles are classes in `@layer components` of `styles.css` (`main-button`, `pill-button`, `input-field`, `paper`, …). A class name must not match a utility Tailwind generates from a theme colour: a `.text-field` class got the `text-field` utility generated from `--color-field` as well, which painted the input's text white on a white field. The input class is `.input-field`.
- The UI is in Spanish; code is in English.

### 2.3 Comportamiento crítico · settled

El texto en blanco se rechaza en el schema del contract: `text` lleva un check de que tenga algo más que espacios y saltos de línea, así que un `text` vacío o en blanco responde `400` antes de llegar al handler, y `Polls.vote` guarda el valor tal como llega. La web usa el mismo check para no mandar `text` cuando el campo queda en blanco. Un texto con contenido se guarda con sus espacios: el diseño pide no recortar. (Cambio del test design, Q4: antes el core sacaba el texto vacío y lo guardaba con el punto solo.)

Los resultados del alumno se niegan en `forStudent` y no en `tally`: `tally` sigue contando el feedback para el profe (3), y el alumno no ve resultados porque su encuesta nunca entra en `shown`. Como `counts` recibe solo `shown`, la query de conteos tampoco lee respuestas de feedback para el alumno.

`PATCH /api/admin/polls/:id` devuelve la encuesta por el mismo `forTeacher`, así que un feedback recién activado o cerrado vuelve con sus barras y su lista. `POST /api/admin/polls` arma la encuesta nueva sin pasar por `forTeacher`, con `tally(poll, noResponses)`; un borrador de feedback vuelve con cinco ceros y `responses: []`. El alumno nunca recibe la clave: `forStudent` arma `Poll`, que no la tiene. La regla: el profe recibe, en cada encuesta de feedback, cuántos eligieron cada punto, y el nombre, el avatar, el punto y el texto de cada alumno que respondió, en el orden de la primera respuesta; la query que cuenta nunca lee el texto.

## 4 Tarjeta de feedback del alumno · inicio y aula

### 4.1 Screen layout · settled

El prototipo `../prototypes/feedback.html` muestra los seis estados y no cambia en esta rama. El estado que lleva el cambio es "sin responder":

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│   [ card de la sesión: título, resumen, links ]          │
│   [ encuestas activas de otros tipos ]                   │
│   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ ← PollCard
│   │  icon  prompt                                      │ │
│   │  meta                                              │ │ ← pollMeta
│   │  ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐                          │ │ ← FeedbackScale
│   │  └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                          │ │
│   │  label            label             label          │ │
│   │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │ │ ← FeedbackForm
│   │  │  textarea                                    │  │ │
│   │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │ │
│   │                                       [ button ]   │ │
│   └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Enviando: los emojis y el campo se deshabilitan y el botón muestra el spinner. Error: `InlineError` entre el campo y el botón, con lo cargado intacto. Respondido: `FeedbackAnswer` con el emoji, el texto o "Sin comentario.", el agradecimiento y "Cambiar mi respuesta". Editando: el formulario con lo que había mandado, el botón "Modificar feedback" y "Cancelar". Cerrada: `FeedbackAnswer` sin el enlace, o "No respondiste esta encuesta.". La misma tarjeta aparece en el aula, en la pestaña Encuestas, y entre las cerradas del alumno.

### 4.2 Component tree · settled

```
ActivePolls · StudentPollsTab · StudentClassroomSkeleton     sin cambios
└── PollCard                                                 touched
    └── VoteForm                                             touched
        └── FeedbackForm                                     new
            ├── FeedbackScale                                new
            └── FeedbackAnswer                               new

ClosedPolls                                                  touched
└── PollCard                                                 touched
    └── FeedbackAnswer · cerrada                             new
```

**PollCard** elige el ícono del encabezado por el tipo: `chat-messages` para el feedback, `chart-bar` para el resto. Sigue siendo la única tarjeta de los dos lados (wiki web).

**VoteForm** devuelve `FeedbackForm` cuando la encuesta es de feedback, igual que ya separa la word cloud en su propia rama. Así ninguna pantalla que muestra encuestas activas cambia.

**FeedbackForm** muestra el formulario, el estado de gracias y el de edición. Tiene el estado local: `isEditing`, el punto y el texto. `isEditing` separa, en un alumno que ya respondió, el estado de gracias del formulario de edición; sigue el patrón de `changing` en `VoteForm`, con el nombre de booleano del proyecto. Existe aparte de `VoteForm` porque su formulario tiene dos campos y un botón de envío, y la elección y la escala mandan con un toque.

**FeedbackScale** dibuja los cinco emojis como un `radiogroup` y los tres textos de los extremos. Es una pieza propia porque `FeedbackForm` la usa en el formulario nuevo y en la edición con un punto distinto.

**FeedbackAnswer** dibuja una respuesta mandada: el emoji, el texto o "Sin comentario." y la línea de abajo. Recibe la respuesta, si la encuesta está cerrada y un slot `<action>` para "Cambiar mi respuesta". La usan `FeedbackForm` y `ClosedPolls`.

**ClosedPolls** le pasa a `PollCard` un `body` con `FeedbackAnswer` cuando la encuesta es de feedback, porque esa encuesta no tiene resultados que mostrar.

`pick` y `text` arrancan de la respuesta guardada, así que "Cambiar mi respuesta" abre el formulario con lo que el alumno mandó. # Callstack

The path one request takes through the parts of a program: which part receives it, which parts it calls in turn, which condition decides between paths, and where a value the change touches enters, is read and lands.

## What it covers

The entry the request comes in through and what it is given. Each call from one part to the next, nested under its caller. The conditions that split the calls into paths, stated in words. On each path, the values the change adds, reads or passes on, and the call where each one is assembled. Other entries that reach the same parts, and what each passes.

It does not cover how a part reaches its result inside its own body, which is a derivation ledger or prose, nor the full shape of what crosses between parts, which is the interfaces.

## What to check before proposing

- Read the entry point and follow its calls down to the last one the change touches, in the code as it stands.
- Find every other caller of the parts the change touches, and what each one passes.
- Find where each value the change touches is assembled from several fields, and whether every path includes it.
- Check the standards for how the layers call each other, so the proposed path follows them.

## Representation

A plain text tree in a fenced block, from the entry down to the last call the branch touches. The root is the entry with what it is given on the next line. Each nested line is a part and the operation it performs, indented under its caller, with the values the change touches in parentheses. A condition that splits the calls is a line of its own, in words, with the paths under it. Where a call assembles a value, the line spells the fields inline, never through a constant.

The first column marks each line as a diff: `+` for a line the branch adds, `-` for a line it removes, a space for a line both versions have. A line the branch alters is two lines, the `-` one as it stands and the `+` one as it will be, one under the other, so the tree read without the `+` lines is the path today and without the `-` lines the path after the change. A right-hand annotation says what a line does with a value the change touches, such as reading the new field or leaving it out; a line that does nothing with one carries none. Each line naming a part that exists ends with its reference, as `basics` writes one; a part the branch creates has none, because it has no code yet. The tree is not drawn in mermaid, because the diff column and the annotations are half the content and mermaid has no form that can show them.

```
 <entry, with what it is given>                                          [[<path>#<entry>]]
-given {<field>, <field>}
+given {<field>, <field>, <new field>?}
 │
-└─ <part>.<operation>()                                                 [[<path>#<part>.<operation>]]
+└─ <part>.<operation>(<new field>)            ← reads the new field     [[<path>#<part>.<operation>]]
    ├─ <store>.<read>                                                    [[<path>#<store>.<read>]]
    │
    ├─ when <condition>
    │  └─ <part>.<other operation>                                       [[<path>#<part>.<other operation>]]
    │     └─ value = { a, b, c }               new field never included
    │     └─ <store>.<write>(value)                                      [[<path>#<store>.<write>]]
    │
    └─ otherwise
-      └─ value = { a, b }
+      └─ value = { a, b, new field }
+      └─ <part>.<new check>(value)
       └─ <store>.<write>(value)                                         [[<path>#<store>.<write>]]
```

The prose under the tree names the other entries that reach the same parts and what each passes, in words. Then it states the rule the tree implements, once, and what each path ends up carrying. It does not restate the tree.

## When it fits

When the decision is where a value enters, which path it takes and where it lands, inside one request that crosses layers. When several paths assemble the same thing and the change has to reach all of them. A change confined to one part with no callers to show needs no callstack; the prose carries it alone. A change to the order of steps or to what ends a run is a control flow.
# Standards

The conventions that govern the implementation of one root, and what each one governs in it.

## What it covers

Every source of conventions the root's settled branches touch: the wiki entries for the technologies involved, the project's `CLAUDE.md`, `.mahou/basics.md` and any rule file the repository keeps. Each source is listed with the piece of the change it constrains. A source the change does not touch is not listed.

## What to check before proposing

- Derive the list from the branches settled under the root.
- Read each source named before writing its line.

## Representation

One line per source, named by its path or wiki entry, followed by what it governs in this root, stated in terms of the root's settled branches: the declaration, the refactor, the emission, the gate. A reader can go from a source to the piece of the change it constrains and back.

```
- wiki `<topic>/<entry>`: the payload validation at the endpoint
- `CLAUDE.md`, "Testing": where the new tests live and how they are named
- `.mahou/basics.md`: the error format the new endpoint returns
```

## When it fits

Once per root, always, after every other branch. A root closes only when this list exists. Mark the list settled as soon as it is written; do not ask the user to confirm it.
# Screen layout

A low-resolution sketch of the screen the branch changes, with each element drawn as a box in the position it occupies.

## What it covers

Where what the branch adds or alters sits on the screen, and which component renders each piece. The rest of the screen appears only as much as it takes to place the change.

It does not cover who owns what, which is the component tree, nor where the values come from, which is the derivation ledger.

## What to check before proposing

- Read the screen as it renders today, and the components that render the region the change lands in.
- Open the screen's prototype, or create one when the screen has none. Reconcile the prototype with what the design and the branch settled, and iterate it with the user until it shows the final screen. Then sketch the screen that the prototype settled, with its parts, states and copy.
- Check the standards for layout and component conventions, so the proposed placement follows them.

## Representation

Boxes in a fenced block, with nothing inside a box but the word that names what it holds: a title, a label, a value, a bar. No copy, no data, no styling. The sketch draws what the branch adds or alters, each box with an arrow on the right naming the component that renders it. Everything else is one bracketed line per region.

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│   [ existing region, one line per region ]             │
│                         ⋮                              │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │ ← NewComponent
│   │  title                                          │  │
│   │  description                                    │  │
│   │                                                 │  │
│   │  ▓▓▓▓│▓▓▓│▓▓│                                   │  │ ← NewChildComponent
│   │  label  label  label                            │  │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│   [ existing actions ]                                 │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

When the element has several states, sketch the one that carries the change and say in a line how the others differ. The prose under it covers what the sketch cannot place, such as anything whose position depends on the data. When the rendering itself is undecided, the branch goes through the `prototype` skill, and the sketch records what the prototype settled.

## When it fits

A branch that adds or moves something a user sees. It opens a screen branch, before the component tree, because a correction here costs one redrawn sketch. It does not fit a branch with no screen.
